item.title: Anthropic set to begin trading as a US$1.5-trillion company in the biggest IPO on record
item.description: Anthropic is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday after pricing its IPO at US$83 per share, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion and surpassing SpaceX as the largest ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — The artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened for trading Thursday in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite investor fears of a possible AI bubble and public anxiety that the technology threatens lives and livelihoods. Anthropic shares began trading at US$111.50, spiking more than 30 per cent above the initial public offering price. A day earlier, the company priced its IPO at US$83 per share, enough to value the entire business at US$1.5 trillion, surpassing SpaceX as the largest IPO on record. At the start of trading, the valuation leaped to US$2.01 trillion. The debut price was surprising high given investor worries had ratcheted up even more recently following the stunning ouster of AI’s chief promoter, the CEO of Nvidia, amid a possible Chinese spying scandal. Anthropic had earlier set a much lower price range between US$70 to US$78 per share. “It’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia,” said Dan Ives, a financial analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co. “The pricing shows strong demand among investors.” A big test remains if investors maintain the classic “IPO pop” by keeping the stock aloft in its first day — or if it will tumble by the close. Anthropic said it is offering 980 million shares to the public, mostly from the company but also from early investors and stockholders. At US$83 per share, that translates into proceeds of US$81 billion, positioning Anthropic ahead of SpaceX, which raised about US$75 billion in June. The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt In addition to market jitters over AI, the IPO is facing down a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. For its part, Anthropic rival OpenAI decided to postpone its initial offering until next year. Then there are big financial challenges ahead for the company. Anthropic already has taken on US$6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited. While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend US$900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including US$70 billion in the next 12 months. An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability. Anthropic’s IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei. AI industry faces concerns about data centres, a possible bubble and regulations Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector. Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months. In comments at the opening bell Thursday, Amodei sought to dampen fears by stressing a commitment to ensure humans are in control of the technology. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same,” he said. ”The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time.” Amid mounting fears, the regulatory environment could change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centres. And two big states offering incentives for data centres, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction. In his comments Thursday, Amodei also touted a range of positive uses for AI, noting that Claude already is helping scientists do quicker research and that the technology could help accelerate that progress in the future. “Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox and polio history for most of the world,” he said, “but progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families.” He also pointed to Claude’s use across companies, nonprofits and government services. “I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future,” he said. Adding to the pressure to go public was the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently. Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group. “Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & the World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.” ___ Bernard Condon and Barbara Ortutay, The Associated Press Ortutay reported from Oakland, California. Associated Press business writers Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles and Michelle Chapman in New York contributed.

item.title: LeBlanc to chair first meeting of Canada-U.S. advisory committee since midterms
item.description: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is set to hold the first meeting of an advisory committee on bilateral economic relations since the midterm elections that delivered a sharp rebuke of the ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA -- Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc is set to hold the first meeting of an advisory committee on economic relations with the United States since the midterm elections that delivered a sharp rebuke of the Trump administration. LeBlanc’s office confirmed the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations will hold a virtual meeting Thursday. The committee, which includes representatives of the business community, trade organizations and organized labour, met last in October. Canadian Ambassador to the United States Mark Wiseman and Canada’s chief trade negotiator Janice Charette will also be in attendance. U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada rapidly escalated after negotiations broke down in August. Ottawa and Washington each accused the other of putting eleventh-hour demands on the table. Prime Minister Mark Carney said at the time that Trump’s team wanted to restrict Canada’s ability to make trade deals with other countries, endanger Canada’s protections for language and culture, and maintain hefty tariffs on some automobiles. In response, Trump hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs and banned imports of others. He threatened to further increase duties in January if no deal is made by then. The president also signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America. The Trump administration’s tone on Canada softened somewhat after midterm election exit polling indicated that Trump’s trade war and his sweeping tariff agenda were unpopular with American voters. Carney and Trump met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific economic summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. Following the meeting, the prime minister said a “very good trade arrangement” with the United States is possible but Canada won’t just sit around and wait. During a meeting Tuesday of the House of Commons international trade committee in Ottawa, LeBlanc and Charette told MPs a deal was still possible. They cautioned there is no guarantee Canada can restore the terms of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade. Charette said Canada has to prepare for a world where a tariff-free arrangement may no longer be possible. The objective is to “get to the lowest rate of tariff on the narrowest basket of goods with the most preferential access for Canadian businesses and Canadian workers,” Charette said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026. By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

item.title: S&P/TSX composite index down, Nasdaq higher, ahead of trading in Anthropic shares
item.description: Canada’s main stock index was down nearly 300 points and U.S. stock markets were mixed with the tech-heavy Nasdaq higher ahead of the Anthropic launch.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index was down nearly 300 points and U.S. stock markets were mixed in late-morning trading with the tech-heavy Nasdaq higher ahead of the launch of shares in Anthropic. The AI company was set to make its stock market debut today in the biggest public stock offering ever, despite recent investor worries about the sector. The S&P/TSX composite index was down 278.77 points at 34,299.28. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 484.20 points at 49,713.97. The S&P 500 index was down 17.69 points at 7,305.94, while the Nasdaq composite was up 49.05 points at 24,478.94. The Canadian dollar traded for 69.88 cents US compared with 69.80 cents US on Wednesday. The January crude oil contract was up US$1.02 at US$83.33 per barrel, while the December gold contract was down US$64.70 at US$3,677.20 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 19, 2026.

item.title: Tax-loss selling – when does it make sense to sell at a loss?: Stan Wong
item.description: When I review a stock that’s down, I look at what’s changed in the earnings outlook, what the lower price already reflects and where else I could put the money. If the case for owning it has weakened, ...
item.content:encoded:
A stock you bought at $50 now trades at $35. If you had the cash today, would you buy it at $35? When I review a stock that’s down, I look at what’s changed in the earnings outlook, what the lower price already reflects and where else I could put the money. If the case for owning it has weakened, it may be time to sell.

If you’ve decided to sell, the loss may still be worth something at tax time. If you hold the stock in a non-registered account, you can generally use the realized loss to offset capital gains. Losses inside a TFSA, RRSP or other registered account can’t be used this way. Why year-end timing matters To use a loss against this year’s gains, the sale must settle before year-end. Wednesday, Dec. 30, 2026, is the last trading day to sell most stocks and ETFs listed in Canada (TSX and TSX Venture) or the U.S. (NYSE and Nasdaq) for a sale to count in the 2026 Canadian tax year. These trades normally settle one business day later, on Thursday, Dec. 31. Work out what the loss can offset Suppose you realized a $20,000 capital gain earlier this year. You then sell another investment in a non-registered account for an $8,000 capital loss. That brings your net capital gain to $12,000 before applying the capital gains inclusion rate. If your capital losses exceed your gains this year, you can generally carry the net capital loss back to offset taxable capital gains from any of the previous three years or carry it forward indefinitely. For a loss realized in 2026, that means looking back at 2023, 2024 and 2025. A gain from selling a cottage or rental property may be easy to overlook when you’re focused on your brokerage statement. Confirm you have a loss in Canadian dollars A U.S. stock can fall five per cent and still leave you with a capital gain in Canadian dollars. Say you bought it at US$100 when one U.S. dollar was worth $1.30, then sold it at US$95 when the exchange rate was $1.40. Your cost was $130 and your proceeds were $133 per share, leaving a small capital gain before trading costs. Before placing a trade, verify the investment’s adjusted cost base. If you bought the same stock at different prices, generally use the weighted average across your non-registered accounts. Look across accounts before you sell Canada’s superficial loss rule can deny the loss if you or an affiliated person, such as your spouse or common-law partner, buys the same or an identical investment within 30 calendar days before or after the sale, and either of you still owns it 30 days after the sale. Check both partners’ accounts for recent trades and scheduled purchases, including dividend reinvestments. If you contribute an investment at a loss directly from a non-registered account to your TFSA or RRSP, you give up the capital loss. Selling it first and contributing cash, if you have contribution room, can preserve the loss, provided the superficial loss rule doesn’t apply. Keep the exposure you still want If you sell a stock at a loss but still see opportunity in its industry, you could reinvest the proceeds in a peer with a similar business. Consider whether its earnings outlook and valuation justify the purchase. You could also buy a diversified sector ETF that holds the stock you sold. That would give you some exposure if the original stock rebounds while spreading the investment across several companies. A Canadian depositary receipt (CDR), however, represents a direct interest in the underlying shares. If those are the same shares you sold, the CDR can be treated as identical property and trigger the superficial loss rule. Tax-loss selling can be part of a total wealth plan, whether you’re trimming a concentrated position or raising cash for a planned expense. Your tax advisor can help you assess the value of the loss, and your wealth advisor can help you decide where the proceeds would serve you best. If you’re still weighing whether to sell, start where we began. Would you buy the stock at today’s price? Related Stories Tech and AI are under pressure.
